title: Is KYB verification required for every new vendor?
summary: Is KYB verification required for every new vendor? No. Learn when legal duties, bank rules, and vendor risk require checks before you approve payment.

01


**TL;DR**


- Is KYB verification required for every new vendor? No; legal duties depend on the relationship and applicable rules.
- FinCEN customer due diligence requirements do not automatically extend to every ordinary supplier relationship.
- Sanctions compliance and vendor due diligence are separate obligations; a registered business can still present sanctions risk.
- Infinite combines compliance/KYB screening with business accounts and cross-border payment routing for global businesses.


02


## Is KYB verification required for every new vendor?


**No universal U.S. rule requires every company to complete the same KYB process for every supplier.** In 2026, distinguish an ordinary procurement relationship from a relationship subject to financial-services customer due diligence. Then check whether another law, contract, or internal policy imposes additional verification requirements.


The following comparison separates those situations. These are assessment categories, not automatic legal conclusions about a particular vendor.


**Ordinary supplier paid for goods or services**


- What determines the requirement?: Applicable law, procurement policy, contracts, and sanctions exposure
- Recommended approach and best fit: Basic identity and payment checks; best for straightforward procurement relationships
- Benefit: Establishes who you are paying without treating every supplier as an account customer
- Limitation: Does not resolve complex ownership or regulated-activity questions


**Business opening a financial account**


- What determines the requirement?: The institution’s customer-identification and due-diligence obligations
- Recommended approach and best fit: Required customer onboarding; best for account relationships covered by those rules
- Benefit: Connects verification to a defined legal obligation
- Limitation: Does not establish that every unrelated supplier needs identical checks


**Vendor with opaque ownership or inconsistent records**


- What determines the requirement?: The unresolved facts and your applicable obligations
- Recommended approach and best fit: Escalated review; best for relationships that cannot be understood from basic records
- Benefit: Gives reviewers a way to resolve material concerns
- Limitation: Requires additional evidence and an accountable decision-maker


**Vendor subject to payment-provider conditions**


- What determines the requirement?: The provider’s onboarding and transaction requirements
- Recommended approach and best fit: Provider-required verification; best for payments dependent on that provider
- Benefit: Addresses conditions that can prevent payment execution
- Limitation: Provider approval does not replace your own legal responsibilities


For implementation, the guide to[automatically running KYB checks when onboarding a new vendor](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/automatically-run-kyb-checks-when-onboarding-a-new-vendor) addresses the workflow side. First decide which checks apply; only then decide which steps to automate.


03


## Why this matters


Requiring a full ownership investigation for every supplier creates unnecessary work when the relationship does not call for it. Requiring nothing creates a different problem: your team cannot explain who received the money or why the payment was approved.


**Set the verification standard before the first payment, not after a bank asks questions.** Your 2026 vendor policy should separate legal obligations, payment-provider conditions, and discretionary fraud controls. That separation makes exceptions easier to evaluate without describing every internal preference as a legal requirement.


04


## Ordinary suppliers: verify the relationship without inventing a legal duty


For a straightforward supplier, start with the legal business name, registration information where applicable, business address, and payment instructions. Compare the information across the contract, invoice, and available official records. Resolve inconsistencies rather than collecting documents that nobody reviews.


These checks serve different purposes. A registry entry supports the existence of a legal entity; an independently confirmed bank-detail change helps address payment fraud. Neither alone proves that the company’s owners are acceptable or that a particular transaction is lawful.


**Best for ordinary procurement: a documented baseline with clear escalation triggers.** Its advantage is proportionality. Its limitation is that basic checks stop being sufficient when ownership, location, business activity, or payment instructions remain unexplained.


Do not confuse a tax form with completed KYB. Tax documentation addresses tax reporting and classification questions; it does not, by itself, establish ownership, screen sanctions exposure, or authenticate new beneficiary details.


05


## Financial-account customers: apply the rules for that relationship


A vendor can also become a customer of a financial service. For example, a business receiving platform payouts might separately open an account or enter another covered financial relationship. The legal analysis follows that relationship, not the label in your procurement system.


FinCEN’s customer due diligence framework for covered financial institutions distinguishes ownership from control. Under its standard beneficial-ownership definition, the ownership prong generally concerns individuals holding **25% or more** of a legal entity customer, while the control prong identifies **1 individual** with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct the entity. Exclusions, exemptions, and applicable relief must be checked before applying that framework.


These are financial-institution customer-due-diligence concepts, not a universal supplier checklist. In a 2026 onboarding policy, identify which institution owns the obligation and which requirements your agreement passes to your business.


**Best for covered account relationships: the institution’s applicable onboarding process.** The benefit is a defined compliance standard; the limitation is that copying the process into procurement does not establish that it is legally required there.


06


## Ownership concerns: escalate before approving the vendor


Escalated review is appropriate when the information needed to understand a vendor remains unresolved. Examples include conflicting entity names, unexplained ownership layers, or payment requests involving a different entity from the contracted supplier.


Request evidence that answers the specific concern. An ownership chart helps explain a corporate chain, but supporting records are still needed to assess whether the chart is accurate. Additional documents are useful only when they resolve an identified question.


**Best for unresolved ownership concerns: a named reviewer and a recorded decision.** This approach creates accountability. Its limitation is that a review cannot turn missing or contradictory evidence into a reliable finding merely by marking the file complete.


Avoid treating incorporation abroad as proof of wrongdoing. Assess the actual entity, ownership, jurisdiction, business activity, and transaction rather than substituting a geographic stereotype for evidence.


07


## Why vendor verification requirements vary


Your 2026 verification standard should reflect the relationship you actually have. Document these factors in the onboarding decision:


- **Regulated activity:** Determine whether your business or a participating financial institution has customer-identification or due-diligence obligations relevant to the relationship.
- **Vendor role:** Distinguish a supplier selling goods from a business opening an account or receiving another financial service.
- **Jurisdiction:** Check the rules applicable to your business, the vendor, and the transaction, including sanctions restrictions.
- **Ownership clarity:** Determine whether you can identify and explain the entity’s ownership and control where required.
- **Payment-provider conditions:** Identify the evidence your bank or payment platform requires before it processes the payment.
- **Unresolved discrepancies:** Escalate mismatched names, unexplained beneficiary changes, or records that do not support the stated relationship.


**A risk-based policy changes review depth; it does not waive mandatory requirements.** If a rule requires a check, a low internal risk score is not a substitute.


08


## How should you decide what to check before payment?


Use a decision process that records both the evidence and the reason for approval. For your 2026 procedure, separate the following stages so that a successful data lookup does not automatically become payment authorization.


1. **Identify the relationship.** Record whether the business is a supplier, account customer, payout recipient, or more than one of these.
2. **Map the obligations.** Identify applicable legal requirements, provider conditions, and internal controls. Assign an owner to unresolved legal questions.
3. **Check the evidence.** Compare identity, ownership where required, sanctions results, and beneficiary information against the relevant standard.
4. **Resolve exceptions.** Route inconsistencies to a reviewer with authority to request evidence, reject the relationship, or approve a documented exception where permitted.
5. **Authorize payment.** Release funds only after the required controls are satisfied and payment instructions have been appropriately confirmed.


*Evidence checks and payment authorization are separate decisions.*


Keep the evidence source, review date, decision, and approver together. That record lets another reviewer understand the outcome without reconstructing it from email threads. Apply retention and access rules appropriate to the information and obligations involved.


09


## Does sanctions screening count as KYB verification?


**Sanctions screening is a distinct control, not a substitute for establishing business identity and ownership where required.** A name match needs investigation; a clean name search does not prove that every relevant restriction has been addressed.


OFAC’s 50 Percent Rule treats entities owned **50% or more** , directly or indirectly and in the aggregate, by blocked persons as blocked even when the entity is not separately named on a sanctions list. Ownership analysis therefore matters beyond checking a vendor’s trading name.


Do not interchange that **50%** sanctions ownership threshold with the **25%** ownership concept in FinCEN’s standard customer due diligence definition. They answer different questions and have different scopes. Apply the relevant rule rather than setting a single ownership threshold for every compliance task.


10


## Can you rely on a bank’s KYB approval?


**A bank’s approval does not automatically satisfy your separate vendor obligations.** Determine what the bank checked, which entity it checked, and whether you are permitted to rely on that work under the rules governing your relationship.


Payment execution and supplier approval also answer different questions. A bank processing a transaction does not establish that your procurement team authenticated an invoice, confirmed a changed beneficiary, or followed its contractual approval process.


Where responsibilities are shared, record them explicitly. Avoid a process in which your team assumes the provider owns verification while the provider’s agreement assigns data collection or review responsibilities to you.


11


## Where a combined banking and screening platform fits


**Infinite is best for global businesses seeking business accounts, compliance/KYB screening, and cross-border payment routing together.** The platform provides USD and multicurrency bank accounts and routes payments through SWIFT, ACH, Fedwire, and RTP with stablecoin settlement.


The relevant benefit is having those functions within the same financial platform. The limit is legal responsibility: using Infinite does not, by itself, determine which checks your business must perform, establish that every supplier is verified, or resolve an ownership discrepancy.


Before adopting Infinite for this workflow, establish who collects evidence, who reviews exceptions, and who authorizes payment. Keep those responsibilities explicit even when screening and payment capabilities are available together.


12


## FAQ


**Is KYB verification required for every new vendor in the United States?**


No, KYB verification is not a blanket U.S. legal requirement for every new vendor. Requirements depend on the relationship, regulated activities, applicable laws, and payment-provider conditions.


**Do I need beneficial ownership information for every supplier?**


No universal rule requires every ordinary business to collect beneficial ownership information for every supplier. Collect it when applicable law, provider requirements, or unresolved ownership risks call for it.


**Is checking a company registration enough to approve a vendor?**


No, a company registration check alone does not establish that a vendor or payment is acceptable. You still need to address applicable sanctions requirements, payment-detail concerns, and any other required checks.


**Does the 25% ownership threshold apply to every vendor?**


The 25% ownership concept belongs to FinCEN’s standard beneficial-ownership definition for covered financial-institution customer due diligence; it is not a universal vendor rule. Check the applicable scope, exclusions, exemptions, and relief before using it.


**Can a vendor be blocked even if its name is not on a sanctions list?**


Yes, an entity can be blocked under OFAC’s 50 Percent Rule without being separately named on a sanctions list. The rule addresses ownership of 50% or more, directly or indirectly and in the aggregate, by blocked persons.


**Do I have to repeat KYB for every vendor payment?**


There is no universal requirement to repeat a full KYB review for every ordinary vendor payment. Apply the transaction controls, monitoring, and refresh requirements relevant to your business, provider, and relationship.


**Does stablecoin settlement remove the need for vendor checks?**


No, stablecoin settlement does not remove applicable vendor-verification or sanctions obligations. Infinite provides compliance/KYB screening alongside cross-border payment routing, but the settlement method does not determine your legal duties.


13


## One last thing


**An approved vendor record should not automatically approve a new beneficiary.** A genuine supplier can be impersonated, and a legitimate relationship does not authenticate an emailed bank-detail change.


For your 2026 payment controls, treat beneficiary changes as a separate approval event. Confirm the request through an independently established contact channel, not solely through the contact details supplied in the change request. This is a fraud-control recommendation, not a claim that every supplier needs a new full KYB review.


This article provides general U.S.-focused information, not legal advice. Have qualified counsel assess the rules that apply to your business and jurisdictions.
